story: The Djang'kawu were three sibling creation ancestors—two sisters and one brother—who created the landscape of Australia and covered it with plants and animals. They journeyed by canoe from the island of Baralku in the east during the night, guided by the Morning Star, and landed at a place called Yalangbara. The sisters, named Bitjiwurrurru and Madalatj, were the custodians of ceremonial law and carried with them digging sticks, feathered headwear, and sacred objects hidden in a basket and in mats. As they traveled, these objects transformed into various landforms. At Yalangbara, they created freshwater wells by plunging their digging sticks into the sand; the sticks then turned into a variety of plant species, while their clap sticks turned into rock formations. At a site called Balma, high among the sand dunes, the sisters gave birth to the first members of the Rirratjingu clan and performed the first ngarra ceremony, one of the region's major ceremonies. During their journey, the siblings encountered a foreign people cooking a sea creature on an island in a bay; the siblings asked them to leave the land. The Djang'kawu then continued westward, producing more offspring, who became the ancestors of other clans belonging to the same moiety.
